title: Balance of Power and Deterrence

cards.h: Two ways states try to stay safe
cards.b:
How do states protect themselves in an anarchic world? Two classic answers: balance of power (match your rival's strength) and deterrence (make attack too costly).

Both are central to realism. Both also shape India's security today, from its response to China's rise to its nuclear posture towards Pakistan.

UPSC asks for meanings, techniques, and critiques. A typical question: "Is balance of power still relevant?" or "Nuclear deterrence has kept the peace. Do you agree?" To answer well, you need Morgenthau, Waltz, Walt and Schelling, a few Cold War examples, and the Indian cases: Kautilya's mandala, the 1998 tests, the stability-instability paradox in South Asia, and the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict.

First we take balance of power, then deterrence.

cards.h: Balance of power: what does it mean?
cards.b:
The term is slippery. Ernst Haas, in "The Balance of Power: Prescription, Concept or Propaganda?" (1953), found eight meanings. Inis Claude, Power and International Relations (1962), grouped them as: a situation (a rough equality of power), a policy (acting to prevent any state from dominating) and a system (a way the international order works).

Core idea

If one state grows too strong, others will join to check it. The result is that no one dominates, and the independence of states survives. History offers examples: Europe against Louis XIV, Napoleon and Hitler.

Assumptions: states are the key actors, they want to survive, power can be measured, and alliances can shift freely.

Morgenthau (1948) listed methods: divide and rule, compensations (territorial trades), arms build-up, alliances, and a "holder of the balance", a swing power like Britain in Europe.

cards.h: Waltz, Walt and the modern debate
cards.b:
• Waltz (Theory of International Politics, 1979): balancing is not a policy choice but a result of the system. Anarchy makes states balance, as firms in a market compete. Balances form whether or not anyone intends them.
  • Internal and external balancing. Internal: build up your own economy and army. External: ally with others.
  • Stephen Walt (The Origins of Alliances, 1987): states balance against threat, not just power. Threat depends on aggregate power, geography, offensive capability and perceived intent. Weak states may bandwagon (join the stronger side).
  • Mearsheimer sees a role for the offshore balancer: a power like the US that stays away from Eurasia but intervenes if a regional hegemon rises.
  • Soft balancing (Robert Pape and T.V. Paul, 2005): using diplomacy and institutions, not alliances, to constrain a strong state. Example: opposition to the 2003 Iraq war.
  • Balance of interests (Randall Schweller): not all states balance, some bandwagon for profit.

• 1648. Peace of Westphalia: sovereign states and the idea of a balance.
  • 1713. Treaty of Utrecht names the balance of power as its aim.
  • 1815. The Concert of Europe after Napoleon (Vienna, Metternich, Castlereagh).
  • 1871-1890. Bismarck's alliance system.
  • 1914. Rigid alliances (Triple Entente and Triple Alliance) turned a Balkan crisis into a world war.
  • 1945-91. Bipolar balance between NATO and the Warsaw Pact.

The lesson from 1914: balancing can fail when alliances are rigid. Alliance entrapment, miscalculation and arms races can turn a balance into a war.

• Vague. It has too many meanings to be a testable theory.
  • Not automatic. States often fail to balance, or balance late. In the 1930s, Britain and France appeased Germany. Others "buck-pass".
  • Dangerous. It rests on calculating power, and misjudgements lead to war (1914). It does not stop arms races.
  • Amoral. Small states were often used as tokens, as in the partitions of Poland.
  • Liberals: institutions and trade, not balance, keep peace. Collective security (next lesson) seeks to replace it.
  • Constructivists: balances depend on perceptions. Wendt: 500 British weapons are less threatening to the US than five North Korean ones.
  • Hard to measure in a world of cyber, finance and technology.

Defenders point to repeated balancing against would-be hegemons, and to the way the Quad, AUKUS (September 2021), NATO's growth (Finland 2023, Sweden 2024) and Russia-China ties are explained by balancing logic.

Deterrence means persuading an adversary not to act by threatening unacceptable costs. It works on the adversary's mind.

  • Bernard Brodie, The Absolute Weapon (1946): since atomic bombs, the aim of military force must be to avert wars, not win them.
  • Albert Wohlstetter, "The Delicate Balance of Terror" (1959): deterrence needs a secure second-strike capability, the ability to retaliate after being hit.
  • Thomas Schelling, The Strategy of Conflict (1960) and Arms and Influence (1966): threats must be credible; commitment and signalling matter; "the threat that leaves something to chance".
  • Glenn Snyder (1961): deterrence by punishment (threaten retaliation) versus deterrence by denial (make the attack fail).

Conditions for success

Capability (can you do it?), credibility (will you?), communication (does the adversary know?), and a rational adversary.

cards.h: Mutually assured destruction and the Cold War
cards.b:
By the 1960s each superpower could destroy the other even after absorbing a first strike. This was mutual assured destruction (MAD), the policy named in US debates under Defense Secretary Robert McNamara.

  • The nuclear triad: land-based missiles, submarine-launched missiles and bombers, to protect the second strike.
  • Flexible response (NATO, 1967): options between surrender and holocaust.
  • Extended deterrence: the US "nuclear umbrella" covering allies.
  • Arms control followed: the ABM Treaty and SALT I (1972), INF (1987), START.
  • Stability-instability paradox (Glenn Snyder, 1965): nuclear stability at the top makes limited conventional or sub-conventional conflict more likely below it.

Did deterrence keep the peace? Supporters: no direct US-Soviet war. Critics: luck (Cuba 1962, the Able Archer scare in 1983), and the risk of accidents. Daniel Ellsberg and Scott Sagan point to near-misses.

Today, new tech (hypersonics, missile defence, cyber, AI) tests the old logic, and New START expired on 5 February 2026.

It works

Waltz: nuclear weapons make war irrational, so more states with weapons can mean less war. India-Pakistan have not fought a full war since Kargil (1999), and even the 2025 conflict ended in days.

It does not always work

  • Rational-actor assumptions may fail: leaders can misread, panic or be fanatical.
  • Credibility is uncertain. Would a state risk its cities for an ally?
  • Terrorists and non-state actors are hard to deter.
  • Cyber attacks are hard to attribute.
  • Sagan: accidents, bad command-and-control, and organisational failure.
  • Moral objection: threatening mass killing is wrong. The 2017 Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons rests on this.

Conventional deterrence also matters. Ukraine had given up its Soviet weapons in 1994 and was invaded in 2014 and 2022, and many cite it as a lesson on the value of deterrence, though the Budapest Memorandum was not a binding guarantee.

• Kautilya's mandala is an old model of balancing: ally with the neighbour's neighbour. The six-fold policy matches balance of power logic.
  • Internal balancing. A nuclear arsenal after 1998, missile programmes (Agni series; Agni-V tested with multiple warheads in March 2024), and the nuclear triad with INS Arihant (the first deterrence patrol in 2018) and INS Arighaat (commissioned 2024).
  • External balancing. The Quad (revived 2017, leaders level from 2021), the 2+2 dialogues, defence pacts with the US (LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA), the Malabar exercise and close ties with France, Japan and Australia. Russia remains an arms supplier.
  • Doctrine. Credible minimum deterrence, no first use, and massive retaliation. Pakistan keeps a first-use option and tactical weapons.
  • Stability-instability paradox in South Asia. The 1999 Kargil war, the 2001 Parliament attack, 26/11 (2008), Uri (2016), Pulwama-Balakot (2019) and Pahalgam-Operation Sindoor (2025). India claims it can respond to terror under the nuclear shadow and says it will not accept "nuclear blackmail".
  • Two-front problem from China and Pakistan.

"Balance of power is both a theory and a policy. Explain with examples."
"Is the balance of power relevant in a world of nuclear weapons and interdependence?"
"Discuss the logic of nuclear deterrence. Has it succeeded?"
"Examine India's nuclear doctrine in the context of deterrence."

Structure: meanings (Haas, Claude), methods (Morgenthau), Waltz and Walt, critique, then deterrence: Brodie, Schelling, second strike, MAD, triad, stability-instability paradox. Add the debate, with Waltz versus Sagan. End with India's mandala, the 1998 tests, the 2003 doctrine and the Sindoor experience.

A balanced finish: balancing and deterrence are tools, not guarantees. Both need diplomacy and arms control alongside.

quiz.w: Collective security is an alternative to balance of power.

quiz.q: Stephen Walt argued that states balance against:
quiz.w: The Origins of Alliances (1987): balance of threat.

o: Joining the stronger or threatening side
quiz.w: Weak states may join the dominant power.

quiz.q: The 'offshore balancer' idea is associated with:
quiz.w: A distant great power intervenes only to stop a regional hegemon.
It was set up at the Congress of Vienna.

quiz.q: The 'second-strike capability' concept was stressed by:

o: Making the attack unlikely to succeed
quiz.w: Snyder (1961) distinguished it from deterrence by punishment.

quiz.q: The stability-instability paradox was proposed by:
quiz.w: Snyder (1965): nuclear stability can encourage lower-level conflict.

o: Credible minimum deterrence and no first use
